title: Body Language Expert Reveals Why You’re Still Invisible
guest: Lorraine K. Lee, LinkedIn Top Voice, keynote speaker and author of Unforgettable Presence (formerly led editorial teams at LinkedIn and Prezi)
summary: Lorraine K. Lee, former LinkedIn and Prezi editorial leader and author of Unforgettable Presence, breaks down the unspoken rules of getting seen, heard and promoted. She covers first impressions and 'resting business face', how to talk about wins without bragging, the 'because' and email-haiku tactics, hand gestures on Zoom, minimizing language to cut, and why promotions must be strategized six months ahead with your manager as an ally.

ideas.idea: First impressions form in a tenth of a second and are mostly non-verbal, so posture, eye contact, a solid handshake and not being on your phone matter before you say a word.
ideas.detail: If an interviewer walks out and you are on your phone, or you open a video call with 'one second, I just have to send this message', you have already signaled distraction. Jean adds a dating parallel: do not look at your phone when your date goes to the bathroom.

ideas.idea: Fix 'resting business face' on video by smiling, nodding slowly and raising your eyebrows, because neutral expressions read as angry on camera.
ideas.detail: At home we are relaxed and not thinking about our faces, and video magnifies that. Cherie notes this is especially pertinent for women, who are societally expected to exude warmth; Lee says perception is reality and the skill becomes natural with practice.

ideas.idea: Hard work does not speak for itself; you must be vocal about your work, and using 'we' language makes you sound more senior than 'I' statements.
ideas.detail: Harvard Business Review data shows collaborative language reads as more senior while heavy 'I' statements read as junior. Frame wins as team learnings, ground them in data and tie them to the company's bottom line.

ideas.idea: Find where the decision makers are already showing up, like the company intranet or a Slack channel with the CEO, and post your wins there rather than only in your small team channel.
ideas.detail: When Prezi lacked LinkedIn's team win-announcement emails, Lee asked her boss how to reach everyone and used the company intranet instead. Target the right people at the right time rather than always going wide.

ideas.idea: Repeat things seven times in seven different ways, because a single 10am Slack message misses APAC, Europe and everyone drowning in messages.
ideas.detail: Her former CEO's rule; send it in Slack, then email, then mention it in the team meeting so people do not miss it.

ideas.idea: Sharing an individual accomplishment stops feeling cringe when you frame it as what was hard and what you learned so it is useful to others.
ideas.detail: Jean says group wins were easy to promote because she wanted her team credited, but solo wins felt unnatural until she reframed them as context that helps people; everyone likes a helpful teammate.

ideas.idea: LinkedIn content has three pillars, personal, professional and educational, plus a bonus promotional one, and mixing them buffers the 'I'm humbled and honored' bragging tone.
ideas.detail: Most people start with educational, then professional industry commentary; personal stories are hardest but resonate most, and you can build up to them over time.

ideas.idea: Nothing on LinkedIn is original, so stop waiting for a perfect thought; people stand out through their own experiences and packaging.
ideas.detail: The most common question she gets is from people hesitant to click post; the content is all the same, the people and framing differ. Jean admits she never posts and only drafts off Cherie's tags.

ideas.idea: Adding the word 'because' to a request increases compliance by up to 93%, even when the reason is weak.
ideas.detail: Use it for deadlines: 'fill this out by Friday because I'm excited to share what you did with the company' or 'because I'm out Friday'. Cherie recalls the Xerox copier line study where 'because I need to make copies' still got people to yield, and a friend's mom who asks for discounts at Louis Vuitton just 'because'.

ideas.idea: Write an 'email haiku': a message concise enough to fit on a smartphone screen without scrolling, respecting the recipient's time.
ideas.detail: The idea comes from Kim Scott, author of Radical Candor, one of three dozen leaders Lee interviewed for her book. Spending 20-30 extra minutes eliminating the excess avoids back-and-forth clarification and makes teams more productive.

ideas.idea: The subject line is prime real estate and your email's first impression; tag it 'action needed', 'FYI, no response needed' or 'due April 7'.
ideas.detail: Jean cites Stanford's Winning Writing class with Glenn Kramon, a 37-year New York Times editor, on email hygiene since people read on phones. Cherie says in finance they wrote the whole message in the subject line ending with EOM (end of message), a power move.

ideas.idea: Showing your hands on video makes you appear warmer, more energetic and more trustworthy, and gestures raise recall of what you say by 33%.
ideas.detail: Frame the camera with three to five fingers of space above your head and show some torso, then lift your hands slightly higher than feels natural so they are visible instead of twitching shoulders. Cherie compares the added movement to CoComelon changing the screen every two seconds, and says gesturing can trick her into higher energy on low-energy Zooms.

ideas.idea: On stage, match your hand movements and gaze to your message, e.g. counting one-two-three or placing each point in a different part of the room, so vocal and visual align.
ideas.detail: From a Stanford executive presence and public speaking lecture Jean took; it makes you seem locked into and believing your own message.

ideas.idea: Cut minimizing language: replace 'does that make sense?' with 'let me know if you have any questions', 'sorry I'm late' with 'thank you for your patience', and 'I think' with 'I recommend' or 'the data suggests'.
ideas.detail: 'Does that make sense' is the phrase everyone in her workshops admits using three times a day; it implies you are unsure of what you just said, while the swap stays collaborative but confident. Small tweaks compound into more authority over time.

ideas.idea: Loud people get promoted because they are visible, so the answer is not to be loud but to be strategic and make your own voice heard with substance.
ideas.detail: Someone promoted only for being loud eventually stalls because they cannot back it up; do not let the loud annoying guy be a cloud over you, become the CEO of your own career.

ideas.idea: Start the promotion conversation six months before review time, know who else is in the room, and close the skill gaps that could block you.
ideas.detail: Lee did not realize early on that other people beyond her manager decide promotions or that raising it when writing her review was far too late. Jean, speaking as a former manager, describes the legwork: identifying who must vote yes, who will object and how to mollify them months ahead.

ideas.idea: Explicitly tell your manager you want to be promoted, and repeat it, because many people are content where they are and managers will not assume ambition.
ideas.detail: Bringing the manager in early makes it a joint plan and lets them plant seeds and advocate on your behalf; it is a lot of work for them, so they must be invested.

ideas.idea: Your boss does not have to like your personality, but they must like what you bring and you must make their life ten times easier.
ideas.detail: Whether through a sunny disposition or being a 10x performer, your manager has to respect your work enough to do the behind-the-scenes labor a promotion requires.
